quote: Compare it to Taiwan, a country with about the same population – and a similar size economy – that faces a vastly larger security threat. We are spending as much as twice what Taiwan spends on military expenditure.
summary: Australia spends as much as twice what Taiwan, a country with a similar-sized economy, spends on its military.

factCheck.title: Military spend comparison problematic, say experts

findings: Stockholm International Peace Research Institute data for 2023 record Australian military spending of US$32.3 billion against Taiwan's US$16.6 billion, roughly double. Australia's nominal GDP (about US$1.87 trillion) is, however, more than twice Taiwan's (about US$802 billion), so Taiwan spends more as a share of its economy (2.2 per cent against 1.9 per cent). The 'similar size economy' comparison holds only on a purchasing-power-parity basis (CIA World Factbook: Taiwan US$1.14 trillion in 2019, Australia US$1.33 trillion in 2022), which three experts told AAP FactCheck was a problematic basis for comparing military spending because hardware is bought in US dollars and Taiwan relies on conscription. On a consistent purchasing-power basis the Lowy Institute put 2022 spending at US$36.9 billion for Australia and US$30 billion for Taiwan.
context: AAP FactCheck rated other figures in the same video accurate, including that Australia's per-capita military spending had roughly doubled since 2003 and was about three times Japan's and six times China's. A representative for Senator Shoebridge pointed AAP FactCheck to CIA World Factbook purchasing-power-parity GDP figures as the basis for the economic comparison. AAP FactCheck's 'Mixture' rating means the claim includes accurate information but also significant errors or problems.

quote: It allows the government to ban people from certain countries from ever travelling to Australia. The government has not said what countries this will apply to. But it could be literally any country.
summary: The Migration Amendment (Removal and Other Measures) Bill 2024 would let the government ban people from any country from travelling to Australia.
statementContext: Video posted on X describing the Migration Amendment (Removal and Other Measures) Bill 2024 as a 'Trump-style travel ban bill'

factCheck.title: Greens senator David Shoebridge says the government is proposing a law that would allow Trump-style travel bans. Is that correct?

findings: The bill would allow the immigration minister to designate any country a 'removal concern country' if the minister thought it in the national interest, after which that country's citizens outside Australia could not make valid visa applications, with exemptions for dual nationals, the partners, children and parents of Australians, and refugee and humanitarian applicants. The explanatory memorandum describes the designation as a 'discretionary personal power'. Legal experts from the Kaldor Centre, the University of Sydney, the University of Technology Sydney and the University of Queensland, and the Law Council of Australia, told RMIT ABC Fact Check that the discretion was exceptionally broad with very limited scope for judicial review, and broader than the United States visa-sanction power that the Trump administration applied to nine countries between 2017 and 2020, which mostly targeted government officials. One expert noted that a court could strike down an unreasonable designation, so 'literally any country' is not certain in practice.
context: RMIT ABC Fact Check found the claim 'a fair call'. The bill was introduced after the High Court's NZYQ decision ended indefinite immigration detention; the government described the power as a diplomatic tool to encourage countries to accept the return of their nationals. A spokesman for Senator Shoebridge told Fact Check that while there were 'some minor differences' from the Trump-era orders, 'the purpose of the bill is the same'.

quote: selling weapons, after weapons, after weapons to Israel
summary: Australia has been selling weapons after weapons to Israel.
statementContext: Senate, debate to take note of answers to questions without notice

originalSource.title: Senate Hansard, 7 November 2023: questions without notice, take note of answers (Trade: Department of Defence)

factCheck.title: David Shoebridge says Australia has been selling 'weapons, after weapons, after weapons' to Israel. Is that correct?

findings: Defence officials told Senate estimates on 25 October 2023 that 351 export permits relating to Israel had been issued since 1 January 2017, but that permits cover 'military and dual-use' goods such as radios, sporting equipment and vehicle parts, and that none of the 322 permits issued between January 2017 and 31 March 2023 was for 'lethal equipment'. ABS trade data showed exports to Israel in the 'arms and ammunition' category averaging about $2.6 million a year over the five years to 2022 and $8,000 in the first nine months of 2023; Australia's Arms Trade Treaty reports record six 'small arms and light weapons' sent in 2016 and 2017. Defence Minister Richard Marles said on 7 November 2023 that 'Israel has not sought any weapons from Australia and we have not provided any'. Defence analysts told Fact Check the export data are opaque, and an editor's note added on 13 December 2023 said the available data may not capture inputs to international supply chains, such as components for weapons systems.
context: RMIT ABC Fact Check published this analysis in its CheckMate newsletter without a verdict label. PUBLIC RECORD classifies the claim as mixed: the available official data do not show sales of complete weapons to Israel in the period, while the permit system covers a broad range of military and dual-use goods and the data do not capture components supplied through international supply chains. No direct response from Senator Shoebridge to the fact-check is recorded; the Greens subsequently tabled a petition calling for an end to military exports to Israel.
